sn22.87:1.2: Vakkali’s verses describe his perseverance in the face of illness ([thag5.8]()), for which he was said to be the foremost in commitment to faith ([an1.208](), [snp5.19:16.1]()). | Text has _nivesana_, normally “house”, as also at [pli-tv-kd10:2.3.11](). [mn140:3.2]() has the expected _āvesana_, “workshop”.
sn22.87:2.11: Normally “remorse” (_kukkucca_), as one of the five hindrances, is said to arise from a breach of ethics. This passage shows that it can be broader than that.
sn22.87:3.1: The body is both a nest of disease and decay, as well as the site of pleasure and mindfulness in meditation. The Buddha did not look away from the foul aspects of the body, nor was he shy about depicting his own body in the same terms.
sn22.87:3.2: Compare [mn28:28.5](), “one who sees dependent origination sees the teaching”. If you understand the Dhamma you will understand the true nature of the Buddha, which is not his physical form (cf. the _dhammakāya_ at [dn27:9.6]()).
sn22.87:5.4: Remember, he was staying in a potter’s shed, perhaps for access to medical care. But his heart was in the wilderness.
sn22.87:8.36: Compare Godhika at [sn4.23:2.3](), Channa at [mn144:13.11]() = [sn35.87](), and notes at [mn145:5.32]() and [pli-tv-bu-vb-pj3:2.49.1]() = [sn54.9]().
sn22.87:10.6: _Vivatta_ (or _vivaṭṭa_) often means “cast off”, as in “the fetters” (_vivattayi saṁyojanaṁ_) or the “veil” (_vivaṭṭacchada_). Here it describes the dead monk’s body after attaining final Nibbāna.
